intro: Cloud architecture and system design — the two things the job applications need and the two things you are studying anyway. Publishing as you study is the cheapest portfolio there is, and 'I measured this' outranks 'here is what the docs say' on every query below.

groups.title: AWS Solutions Architecture
groups.note: Written while sitting SAA-C03. Each one is revision and a portfolio piece at the same time. Target query is given because the bet is out-specific, not out-rank.

items.t: I rebuilt a Cloudflare Workers app on AWS Lambda — what each costs and where each breaks
items.d: Port one slice of your own system: Workers to Lambda, cron to EventBridge, Durable Object alarms to EventBridge Scheduler, Neon to RDS. Almost nobody has run the same non-trivial workload on both, which makes this the piece only you can write. Query: cloudflare workers vs aws lambda cost comparison.

items.t: A 15-minute RTO costs this much: pricing the four AWS disaster recovery strategies
items.d: Price backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site for one workload, and publish the RTO each actually buys. The four strategies are described everywhere and costed nowhere. Query: aws disaster recovery cost comparison rto rpo.

items.t: Multi-AZ is not a read replica: measuring RDS failover instead of describing it
items.d: Deploy both, force a failover, and time it with a client writing continuously. The most confused distinction in the exam, and every article explains it without a number. Query: rds multi-az vs read replica difference.

items.t: Security groups versus NACLs, proven with packets rather than prose
items.d: Break traffic four ways — SG ingress, SG egress, NACL ingress, NACL egress — and screenshot the flow logs. Stateful versus stateless is a sentence everyone repeats; the dropped return packet is what makes it stick. Query: security group vs nacl stateful stateless.

items.t: The VPC diagram that finally made it click — built in Terraform, not drawn
items.d: Two AZs, public and private subnets, IGW and NAT, with proof that a private instance reaches out and nothing reaches in. Highest-volume query here, and yours ranks only if the repo runs. Query: aws vpc public private subnet nat gateway tutorial.

items.t: Egress is the bill nobody models
items.d: Move a fixed payload cross-AZ, cross-region and out to the internet, then put the three costs side by side per GB. Where real AWS bills go wrong. Query: aws data transfer cost between availability zones.

items.t: S3 lifecycle transitions: where the money actually goes, including retrieval
items.d: Standard to IA to Glacier, charted per GB-month — and then the retrieval cost and time every comparison omits. Query: s3 storage class lifecycle cost glacier retrieval.

items.t: Running a Well-Architected review on your own side project
items.d: The real review against your own system, findings published including the embarrassing ones. Reviews are shared as checklists and never as results. Query: aws well architected framework review example.

groups.title: System design and interview prep — beginner
groups.note: High-intent queries: everyone searching these is preparing for the same interviews you are.

items.t: Turning an awesome-list into a study plan: how to actually read a system design repo
items.d: Take the big starred repos and produce a six-week ordered plan with one narration per topic. Thousands star these and bounce off them; the plan is the product. Query: how to study system design github repo.

items.t: The back-of-envelope numbers every interview assumes you already know
items.d: Build the latency and throughput cheat sheet, then re-measure at least three entries on your own hardware and say where they differ. The canonical list is fifteen years old. Query: latency numbers every programmer should know.

items.t: Reading a system diagram: what the boxes hide
items.d: Take three published architecture diagrams and name, for each arrow, the failure mode it conceals. Teaches the skill interviews actually probe.

groups.title: System design and interview prep — intermediate

items.t: Designing a rate limiter: token bucket versus sliding window, implemented and benchmarked
items.d: Both implemented, burst behaviour and memory measured, with the traffic each lets through that the other blocks. The second most common design question, almost always answered from memory. Query: token bucket vs sliding window rate limiter.

items.t: Idempotency keys: the detail that separates a junior answer from a senior one
items.d: A payment endpoint that survives duplicate submits, client retries, and a crash between write and response — each proven by test. You have already lived this in your own webhook ingress. Query: idempotency key api design retry.

items.t: Caching strategies, measured: write-through, write-back, write-around
items.d: Three implementations over one workload, with hit rates, staleness windows and what each loses on a crash. Universally drawn, never measured. Query: write through vs write back vs write around cache.

items.t: Why 'design a URL shortener' is a trick question
items.d: Build it, then break it where interviewers probe: key collisions, hot keys, analytics writes drowning reads. Enormous volume, uniformly shallow results. Query: url shortener system design interview.

items.t: Webhooks versus APIs — and when polling is the wrong answer
items.d: Push versus pull, delivery guarantees, retries and the cost of each. You replaced a polling loop with a webhook and have the bill to prove the difference.

items.t: API architecture patterns compared
items.d: REST, GraphQL, gRPC and event-driven, judged by what each makes hard rather than what each makes possible.

groups.title: System design and interview prep — advanced

items.t: Consistent hashing, implemented and then rebalanced under load
items.d: A ring with virtual nodes, then add and remove a node under live traffic and chart how many keys move. The rebalance chart is the asset. Query: consistent hashing implementation virtual nodes.

items.t: The outbox pattern: exactly-once that survives a crash between the write and the publish
items.d: Write a row and publish an event atomically, then kill the process mid-flight and show nothing lost and nothing duplicated. The crash test is the whole article. Query: transactional outbox pattern implementation.

items.t: Reading someone else's architecture docs and finding the decision they did not write down
items.d: Take two open-source ADR sets, find a decision implied by the code but absent from the record, and write the missing ADR. Query: how to read architecture decision records adr.

items.t: Why Ethereum split into consensus and execution clients at the Merge
items.d: The separation as an architectural decision with trade-offs, written for a systems audience rather than a crypto one.

items.t: The gossip protocol in blockchains
items.d: Peer discovery, message propagation and the partial-connectivity assumptions underneath. A distributed-systems topic that happens to be blockchain.
